1	EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Americanstar US (also known as Americanstar) operates an existing polyurethane foam manufacturing facility (Facility) located at 401 Precision Drive, in Waco, McLennan County, Texas (Figure 1).   Americanstar produces slabstock polyurethane foam by chemically reacting polyether polyols, diisocyanates, and minor additives. The cured foam is then incorporated into foam mattresses. Processes at the Facility fall within the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code 326150, Urethane and Other Foam Product (except Polystyrene) Manufacturing. 

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) requires Facilities to prepare a Risk Management Plan (RMP), in accordance with 40 CFR Part 68 for processes that use or store certain listed chemicals over the threshold quantity (TQ). The purpose of the RMP is to prevent accidental releases of toxic and flammable chemicals that could harm the public and the environment. Americanstars prior operations have not been subject to RMP, but the Facility plans to install a new process for foam manufacturing which will include quantities of Toluene Diisocyanate (TDI) that exceed the 10,000-pound TQ. The Facility does not store or plan to use flammable chemicals over the TQ.

The new TDI process will use Wannate TDI-80 (TDI-80) as a raw material. TDI-80 is a mixture of two isomers of TDI, specifically 80% of 2,4-toluene diisocyanate (2,4-TDI, CAS # 584-84-9), and 20% of 2,6-toluene diisocyanate (2,6-TDI, CAS # 91-08-7). The Facility will store the TDI in two (2) storage tanks: one (1) with a capacity of 6,340 gallons and one (1) with a capacity of 2,640 gallons, which is equal to 91,000 lbs total based on the density provided in the safety data sheet. The tanks are located indoors on the eastern corner of the Facility. This RMP has been developed based on the worst-case scenario for each of the processes at the Facility per 40 CFR §68.25.  

Process 1 is the TDI unloading process at the Facility. TDI will be de

livered in tanker trucks to the loading dock on the front of the building to the left side, where the TDI will be pumped directly into the storage tanks via ports through the wall of the Facility (Figure 2). Concrete berms would contain any TDI released during unloading with a design capacity of 7,270 gallons. Tankers are expected to have a maximum capacity of 7,000 gallons, indicating the entire contents of a tanker would fit within the containment area. A worst-case release scenario for this process would be the release of the entire 7,000-gallon contents of a tanker. An analysis was performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 which demonstrates that the toxic endpoint will not affect public receptors. 

Process 2 is TDI storage in the larger TDI storage tank and associated piping. The worst-case scenario is a catastrophic failure of this storage tank with a full capacity of 6,340 gallons. This TDI storage tank is located indoors in the foam production area of the building (Figure 2). The TDI tank, and three other horizontal tanks, are surrounded by 16-inch-high concrete walls which provide containment for a volume up to 7,500 gallons. In the event of an accidental release of a full tank, the liquid contents would be contained within this area. The worst-case release scenario analysis performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 indicates that the toxic endpoint will not extend beyond the property and will not affect public receptors. 

Process 3 is TDI storage in the smaller TDI storage tank and associated piping. The worst-case scenario is a catastrophic failure of this storage tank with a full capacity of 2,640 gallons. This TDI storage tank is in the chemical room next to the foam production area of the building (Figure 2). The chemical room houses fifteen (15) vertical storage tanks, containing various materials, including one for TDI storage. Concrete walls provide containment for a volume greater than 8,000 gallons. In the event of an accidental release of a f

ull tank, the liquid contents would be contained within this area. The worst-case release scenario analysis performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 indicates that the toxic endpoint will not extend beyond the property and will not affect public receptors. 

The Facility has not had any accidental releases in the last 5 years which affected public receptors from the existing process, nor the TDI process as it is not yet installed. As mentioned above, the distance to the toxic endpoint associated with a worst-case release is less than the distance to a public receptor. Additionally, Americanstar has submitted notifications to the following local emergency planning and response organizations:

	City of Waco Emergency Management
	McLennan County Local Emergency Planning Commission

Per 40 CFR §68.10(j), any process meeting the following requirements is eligible for a Level 1 RMP:
1.	No accidental releases of a regulated substance in the five years prior to submission of the RMP,
2.	The distance to the toxic or flammable endpoint is less than the distance to any public receptor, and
3.	Emergency response procedures have been coordinated between the stationary source and local emergency planning and response organizations.
All three (3) processes mentioned above meet these eligibility requirements, and therefore qualify as Program 1.

Sections 2 and 3 discuss the Facilitys accidental release prevention and emergency response policies, respectively. The EPA RMP registration forms are included in Section 4 of the RMP. Section 5 contains the assumptions and methodology used to perform the worst-case release scenario analysis. Section 6 describes when the RMP is to be updated. A letter certifying that, to the best of our knowledge, no public receptors would be affected by a release, is provided in Section 7. 

2	ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION

The purpose of the RMP requirements is to prevent accidental releases of toxic and flammable chemicals that could harm the public

and the environment. Americanstar considers the safety of its employees and the surrounding public of paramount importance. As a result, Americanstar has policies and procedures in place to prevent an accidental release, developed by technical experts and leadership at Americanstar. To guide development of safety procedures for handling of the TDI, Americanstar is using resources and documents developed by the Center for Polyurethanes Industry (CPI), housed by the American Chemistry Council. 

The release prevention program is designed to ensure proper working order of the equipment, safe tank filling, and employee safety. The following information on the release prevention program applies to the TDI process including raw material unloading and raw material storage. At the time of writing this initial risk management plan, the new TDI process is not yet fully installed. Some minor adjustments may be necessary to such programs once foam production operations begin in early 2026.

The design of the facility, safety, training and maintenance programs, and operating procedures were adapted from the existing operations at the Facility. An initial assessment of hazards and safety information, including SDSs, industry standards and safety equipment, was included in the facilitys design process.

Safety begins with proper training of all employees in the dangers and appropriate handling of the materials and equipment. Americanstar will ensure all personnel working with or in proximity to hazardous materials are properly trained. Training will include classroom and on the job training and will be conducted annually, during on-boarding, and after any process change or incident. Competency may be assessed through demonstration and practical evaluation. 

New equipment will be inspected upon installation and tested prior to the commencement of manufacturing operations. Preventative maintenance will be performed per manufacturer recommendations, and inspections will be conduct

ed regularly on all tanks, piping, pumps, and manufacturing equipment to ensure the proper working order of all equipment and to minimize the risk of leaks.  

Process controls used for prevention purposes include the inspection of all tankers before and after unloading of raw materials to ensure there are no spills or leaks.  All storage tanks are equipped with temperature sensors and liquid-level sensors to prevent overfilling in accordance with the International Fire Code (IFC) Section 5003.2.7. Secondary containment has been incorporated into the designs of the tank storage and unloading areas. Additional details on the standard operating procedure for TDI unloading and storage are included in Appendix A.


3	EMERGENCY RESPONSE

Each process at the Facility qualifies for RMP Program 1, and Americanstar has coordinated with local agencies to have the Facility included in the community emergency response plan. Further, the Facility is a non-responding stationary source, meaning Americanstar personnel will not respond to a release of a regulated substance. Therefore, per 40 CFR §68.90(b), this RMP does not include the specific emergency response program requirements of §68.95. The Facility will follow the general emergency response procedures discussed below. 

In the unlikely event of a TDI release, employees are to activate the emergency alarm, which is located near the tanks and foam machine or depress the e-stop on the foam chemical pouring equipment. Subsequently, all personnel will be alerted and the building will be evacuated via the office front door to the designated assembly point. As the chemicals are located on the eastern portion of the building, employees will move to the west side of the property, unless it is deemed unsafe due to the wind direction at the time.  

The EHS Manager, who serves as the RMP Emergency Contact, will immediately notify the contracted Spill Cleanup company and the City of Waco Emergency Management, who will coordinate with

the Facility for the safest and quickest response to contain any release, minimizing exposure to emergency responders, employees, and the public.

The SDS indicates TDI vapors are dangerous leading to breathing difficulties or death if inhaled. TDI should only be handled while wearing SDS-specified PPE, including safety glasses, gloves, respirator, chemical protective coveralls, and steel toed shoes. An emergency shower and eye wash station are located by the TDI unloading area in case of exposure.  There will also be spill cleanup and containment supplies stored and staged near the loading/unloading area and by the tanks. These supplies include; ventsorb, air pollution control barrels, salvage drums, and sand. The SDS is included in Appendix B. 

A Program 1 RMP is required to include all of the federal or state emergency plan requirements to which the Facility is subject, per 40 CFR 68.180(a)(3). In addition to RMP, the following emergency management statutes may apply to the Facility:
1)	Emergency Planning and Community Right to Know Act (EPCRA) 40 CFR Section 302
2)	Emergency Action Plan, OSHA, 29 CFR 1910.38
3)	Spill Prevention Control and Countermeasures, 40 CFR 112
4)	Texas Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (TPDES), 30 TAC Chapter 305
5)	Hazard Communication Standard, OSHA, 29 CFR 1910.1200
6)	Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) 40 CFR 261

5	WORST-CASE RELEASE ANALYSIS

EPAs ALOHA model was used to determine the range of exposure of dangerous concentrations in the event of a worst-case scenario for each of the three processes, material unloading and tank storage in two locations. The first scenario is a catastrophic failure of a 7,000-gallon tanker truck while unloading TDI. The second scenario is a catastrophic failure of a 6,340-gallon capacity storage tank of TDI and the third scenario is a catastrophic failure of a 2,640-gallon capacity storage tank containing TDI. The substance to be stored at the Facility is a mixture of 2,4-TDI (80% composition) and 2,6-TDI (20% composition). As a measure of caution, the ALOHA model was run for both 2,4-TDI and 2,6-TDI. The distance to the endpoints for 2,6-TDI were consistently further-reaching than for 2,4-TDI. In an effort to be conservative, the results from 100% composition of 2,6-TDI have been included here. The following is a discussion on the assumptions and parameters input into the ALOHA model.

The location of the Facility is in Waco, TX [31.52° N, 97.17° W]. The elevation at this point is 530 feet above sea level. Guidelines for atmospheric parameters are presented in 40 CFR §68.22. Per §68.22(c), the highest temperature recorded in the past three years at the location is to be used for modeling. Data from the National Climate Data Center indicates the highest temperature recorded in Waco since October 1, 2022, was 110? . The temperature of the substance is assumed to be the same as air temperature. A wind speed of 1.5 m/s was used in accordance with §68.22(b). Partly cloudy skies with no temperature inversion is a climatologically sound assumption. The relative humidity was assumed to be 60% based on the average annual air temperature of 68? and dewpoint of 55? . The atmospheric stability class F was used in accordance with §68.22(b). 

5.1	PROCESS 1 WORST-CASE SCENARIO
A worst-case release scenario analysis was conducted for Process 1 in accorda

nce with §68.28. In this scenario, a spill due to the catastrophic failure of a tanker during the unloading of TDI at the dock on the east corner of the building was considered.  

The model was based on the following parameters: 

	The maximum tanker truck volume is 7,000 gallons. 
	Should a failure occur during unloading, the substance would drain to a containment area capable of holding a volume of 7,218 gallons with an area of 965 square feet [68.9 x 14].
	The endpoint concentration of 0.0070 mg/L for the threat zone was obtained from Part 68 Appendix C.

The ALOHA model was run for Process 1 using 2,6-TDI resulting in the threat zone radius of 26 yards. The closest public receptor is approximately 130 yards to the east. The risk area is depicted in Figure 3. Therefore, a spill of this magnitude would not affect a public receptor. Model output is located in Appendix C.
5.2	PROCESS 2 WORST-CASE SCENARIO
The following parameters were used in the worst-case release scenario analysis for a catastrophic failure of the storage horizontal TDI tank located by the foam production line (Process 2) on the eastern portion of the building.

	This storage tank has a maximum capacity of 6,340 gallons. 
	A concrete secondary containment area surrounding the storage tank has an area of 803 square feet [45.7 × 17.6].
	The endpoint concentration of 0.0070 mg/L for the threat zone was obtained from Part 68 Appendix C.

The ALOHA model was run for Process 2 using 2,6-TDI resulting in the threat zone radius of 24 yards. Results are within the property lines, as the closest boundary is approximately 54 yards to the southeast of the tank location. The risk area is depicted in Figure 3, and model output is located in Appendix C.
5.3	PROCESS 3 WORST-CASE SCENARIO
The following parameters were used in the worst-case release scenario analysis for a catastrophic failure of the storage vertical TDI tank located in the chemical room (Process 3) on the eastern portion of the building

.

	This storage tank has a maximum capacity of 2,640 gallons. 
	A concrete secondary containment area surrounding the storage tank has an area of 1,070 square feet [43.8 × 24.4].
	The endpoint concentration of 0.0070 mg/L for the threat zone was obtained from Part 68 Appendix C.

The ALOHA model was run for Process 3 using 2,6-TDI resulting in the threat zone radius of 30 yards. Results are within the property lines, as the closest boundary is approximately 42 yards to the northeast of the tank location. The risk area is depicted in Figure 3, and model output is located in Appendix C.

6	UPDATES
The RMP will be reviewed periodically with a revised RMP being submitted to the EPA at least every 5 years. The following situations also result in the need to revise and update the RMP:
	When a substance in use at the facility becomes regulated by the EPA;
	Before a regulated substance present in an already covered process is increased above a threshold quantity;
	Before a new process involving a regulated substance above a threshold quantity begins;
	Within 6 months of a change requiring a hazard review;
	 Within 6 months of a change requiring revised offsite consequence analysis; and,
	Within 6 months of a change that alters the process level of a covered process.
